UNIT 11 — The Electromagnetic Spectrum

Physics · Form 4 · MSCE · Malawian Science Books

Everything you see, every radio signal, every X-ray at the hospital, and the warmth you feel from a fire — all of it is the same thing: electromagnetic waves. This unit shows you the full family, from the longest radio wave to the shortest gamma ray.

11.1 The Complete Electromagnetic Spectrum

THE BIG IDEA

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum — 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s (the speed of light). What makes them different is their frequency and wavelength. Arrange them by frequency and you get the electromagnetic spectrum — one continuous family, from radio to gamma.

The seven regions (in order of increasing frequency)

RegionTypical wavelengthTypical frequencySource
Radio waves> 0.1 m< 3 × 10⁹ HzAerials, transmitters
Microwaves1 mm – 0.1 m3 × 10⁹ – 3 × 10¹¹ HzKlystrons, magnetrons
Infrared700 nm – 1 mm3 × 10¹¹ – 4 × 10¹⁴ HzHot objects, LEDs
Visible light400 – 700 nm4 × 10¹⁴ – 7.5 × 10¹⁴ HzSun, lamps
Ultraviolet10 – 400 nm7.5 × 10¹⁴ – 3 × 10¹⁶ HzMercury lamps, Sun
X-rays0.01 – 10 nm3 × 10¹⁶ – 3 × 10¹⁹ HzX-ray tubes
Gamma rays< 0.01 nm> 3 × 10¹⁹ HzRadioactive nuclei

The universal wave equation

Every electromagnetic wave obeys:

c = f λ

where c = speed of light in vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s), f = frequency in hertz (Hz), λ = wavelength in metres (m).

Because c is constant, frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional: as frequency goes up, wavelength goes down.

The visible region

Visible light is a very narrow band. From longest to shortest wavelength: red → orange → yellow → green → blue → indigo → violet.

A handy memory phrase: Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain.

KEY POINTS — 11.1

- All EM waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.

- The spectrum in order of increasing frequency: radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma.

- Frequency and wavelength are linked by c = f λ.

- Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = more energy.

- Visible light is a tiny slice of the whole spectrum.

11.2 Properties of Electromagnetic Waves

THE BIG IDEA

All EM waves share the same core properties. If you know these, you know how any EM wave behaves — whether it is a radio signal or a gamma ray.

Universal properties

- They are transverse waves — the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel.

- They do not need a medium — they travel through a vacuum.

- They all travel at the same speed in a vacuum: c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

- They carry energy from one place to another.

- They can be reflected, refracted, diffracted, and polarised.

- They can be absorbed by matter — the amount depends on the material and the frequency.

- They obey c = f λ.

When they enter a medium

In a material (air, glass, water), EM waves slow down. Their frequency stays the same; their wavelength gets shorter; their speed decreases.

v = f λ (v < c in any material)

KEY POINTS — 11.2

- EM waves are transverse.

- They do not need a medium.

- They travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.

- They transfer energy.

- They can be reflected, refracted, diffracted, polarised, absorbed.

- On entering a medium: speed decreases, wavelength decreases, frequency stays the same.

11.3 Methods of Detecting Electromagnetic Waves

THE BIG IDEA

Our eyes only see visible light. Every other region of the spectrum must be detected with a specific device — each one tuned to that part of the spectrum.

Detectors, region by region

RegionDetector
Radio wavesAerial / antenna + tuned receiver
MicrowavesDipole antenna + crystal detector; mobile phone antenna
InfraredThermopile, bolometer, blackened thermometer, IR camera
Visible lightEye, photographic film, photodiode, CCD/CMOS sensor
UltravioletPhotographic film, fluorescent screen, photoelectric cell
X-raysPhotographic film, fluorescent screen, Geiger–Müller tube
Gamma raysGeiger–Müller tube, scintillation counter, photographic film

KEY POINTS — 11.3

- Radio / microwave → aerial.

- Infrared → thermopile or blackened thermometer.

- Visible → eye or photographic film or photodiode.

- UV → fluorescent screen or photographic film.

- X-ray / gamma → Geiger–Müller tube, scintillation counter, or film badge.

11.4 Applications of Electromagnetic Waves

THE BIG IDEA

Every region of the spectrum is useful. Radio for broadcasting, microwaves for cooking and phones, infrared for remotes and heaters, visible for sight, UV for sterilising, X-rays for medicine, gamma rays for cancer treatment.

RegionEveryday applications
Radio wavesRadio & TV broadcasting, WiFi, mobile phones, radar
MicrowavesMicrowave oven, satellite communication, mobile networks, speed guns
InfraredTV remote control, thermal imaging, security cameras, heaters
Visible lightVision, photography, optical fibres, laser pointers, solar cells
UltravioletSterilising medical equipment, sun tanning, forgery detection
X-raysMedical imaging (bones), airport security, industrial inspection
Gamma raysCancer treatment (radiotherapy), sterilising food, thickness gauges

Why each region does what it does

Higher frequency = higher energy = deeper penetration or stronger biological effect.

- Radio → low energy, passes through walls, safe.

- Microwaves → resonates with water molecules, so heats food.

- Infrared → absorbed by matter, feels as heat.

- Visible → absorbed by pigment in the eye, gives vision.

- UV → ionising enough to kill germs; also causes sunburn.

- X-rays → pass through soft tissue but not bone or metal.

- Gamma → pass through most matter; ionising; kills cells.

KEY POINTS — 11.4

- Radio → communication (broadcast, WiFi, phones).

- Microwave → cooking, satellite links, mobile phones.

- Infrared → remotes, thermal cameras, heaters.

- Visible → sight, fibre optics, solar cells, lasers.

- UV → sterilisation, sun-tan, detecting forgery.

- X-ray → medical imaging, security.

- Gamma → cancer treatment, food sterilisation.

11.5 Effects of Electromagnetic Waves

THE BIG IDEA

EM waves do not just carry information — they can also affect the matter they pass through. Low-frequency waves are mostly harmless; high-frequency waves are ionising and can damage living cells.

Ionising vs non-ionising

TypeWhich regions?Effect
Non-ionisingRadio, microwave, infrared, visibleHeats tissue at most; generally safe in low doses
IonisingUltraviolet (partial), X-rays, gamma raysKnocks electrons out of atoms; damages DNA; can cause cancer

Harmful effects on humans

- UV: sunburn, skin ageing, skin cancer, eye damage (cataracts).

- X-rays: cell damage, cancer risk, sterility if high dose.

- Gamma rays: deep cell damage, radiation sickness, cancer.

- Microwave (high intensity): internal heating, burns.

- Infrared (very high intensity): skin burns, eye damage.

Precautions

- Wear sunscreen and protective clothing in strong sunlight.

- Radiographers stand behind lead shields and wear film badges.

- Don't stare at the sun or bright UV lamps.

- Keep exposure to X-rays as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP principle).

- In Malawi, X-ray and radiotherapy rooms are marked with warning signs and lead-lined walls.

KEY POINTS — 11.5

- Low-frequency EM waves: non-ionising (radio, microwave, IR, visible).

- High-frequency EM waves: ionising (UV, X-ray, gamma).

- Ionising radiation damages DNA → cancer risk.

- UV causes sunburn, ageing, and skin cancer.

- Precautions: sunscreen, lead shields, film badges, ALARP.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Using c = f λ

A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 90 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves. (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)

Step 1. Convert MHz to Hz: 90 MHz = 90 × 10⁶ Hz.

Step 2. Rearrange c = f λ → λ = c / f.

λ = (3.0 × 10⁸) / (90 × 10⁶)

⌈ λ = 3.33 m ⌉

Example 2 — Finding the frequency

Green light has a wavelength of 550 nm. Find its frequency.

Step 1. Convert nm to m: 550 nm = 550 × 10⁻⁹ m = 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ m.

Step 2. f = c / λ.

f = (3.0 × 10⁸) / (5.5 × 10⁻⁷)

⌈ f = 5.45 × 10¹⁴ Hz ⌉

Example 3 — Which wave?

A wave has a wavelength of 0.03 m. Which region of the EM spectrum does it belong to?

Step 1. f = c / λ = (3.0 × 10⁸) / 0.03 = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz.

Step 2. 10¹⁰ Hz lies in the microwave region.

⌈ Microwave ⌉

Full Worked Solutions

Check Yourself — Answers

1. Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

2. 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

3. c = f λ.

4. Infrared.

5. Thermopile (or blackened thermometer, or IR camera).

6. Microwaves.

7. Cancer treatment (radiotherapy), or sterilising equipment.

8. Having enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms, forming ions.

9. Sunburn, skin cancer, ageing, eye damage.

10. Lead absorbs X-rays, protecting the operator from unnecessary exposure.

Exam-Style — Full Solutions

Q1. (a) An EM wave is a transverse wave made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, travelling at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, needing no medium.

(b) Any two: transverse; travel at same speed in vacuum; no medium needed; carry energy; obey c = f λ.

Q2. (a) λ = c / f = (3.0 × 10⁸) / (100 × 10⁶) = 3 m. (b) Radio waves.

Q3. f = c / λ = (3.0 × 10⁸) / (2 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.5 × 10¹⁸ Hz → X-ray region.

Q4. Infrared: thermopile / TV remote. UV: fluorescent screen / sterilising. X-ray: photographic film / medical imaging. Microwaves: dipole antenna / cooking or satellite links.

Q5. (a) Ionising radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms; non-ionising does not. (b) Ionising: gamma. Non-ionising: radio.

Q6. UV has a higher frequency (and hence higher photon energy) than IR, so it is ionising and can damage DNA. IR is non-ionising and mostly just warms tissue.

Q7. (a) X-ray: imaging bones. Gamma: cancer treatment. (b) Stand behind lead shield; wear a film badge; minimise exposure time (ALARP).

Q8. Frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary. Speed decreases in glass, so wavelength (λ = v / f) must also decrease.

Q9. λ = c / f = (3.0 × 10⁸) / (12 × 10⁹) = 0.025 m = 2.5 cm.

Q10. Gamma rays are ionising — they destroy bacteria and viruses on equipment. Radio waves are non-ionising and too low-energy to kill micro-organisms.

Common Mistakes

- Forgetting that frequency does not change when light enters a material (only speed and wavelength change).

- Writing nm or MHz directly into c = f λ without converting to m or Hz.

- Saying X-rays and gamma rays are the same thing — they overlap in wavelength but differ in source (X-rays from electron transitions; gamma from nuclear decay).

- Mixing up which end of the spectrum is dangerous — the high-frequency end is ionising.

- Writing the ROYGBIV order wrong.

- Confusing detectors: an aerial is for radio, a Geiger tube is for ionising radiation.

EXAM TIP

MSCE loves c = f λ calculations. Always: (1) convert units to base SI, (2) rearrange carefully, (3) check the region of the answer.

For 'state one use' questions, name a specific use — not just 'communication', but 'TV broadcasting' or 'mobile phone signals'.

When asked about danger, tie it back to frequency and ionising ability, not just wavelength.

REMEMBER • All EM waves travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. c = f λ always. High frequency = high energy = ionising = dangerous.
